0158               
0159               ; While we don't mean to USE the console ROM, for interrupts we
0160               ; are forced to interface with some of it. We need these addresses
0161               ; to minimize what it does so we can maximize our use of scratchpad.
0162               ; While I'd like to use the cassette hook - requires only 10 instructions
0163               ; and only uses 6 words of scratchpad, we can't here because it
0164               ; loses the return address, meaning you can only use it if you
0165               ; know where your LIMI 2 is and interrupts are otherwise disabled. So
0166               ; we have to use the longer but more standard interrupt hook, which also
0167               ; reads VDP status for us (no choice).
0168               
0169      8379     intcnt              equ >8379   ; interrupt counter byte, adds 1 (from GPLWS r14) every frame
0170      837B     vdp_status          equ >837B   ; VDP status byte mirror
0171      83C2     intwsr1             equ >83c2   ; INT WS R1  - interrupt control flags - must be >8000
0172      83C4     intwsr2             equ >83c4   ; INT WS R2  - address of user interrupt routine (point to int_handler)
0173      83D6     intwsr11            equ >83d6   ; screen timeout counter - must be odd (init to 1, is inct every frame)
0174      83DA     intwsr13            equ >83da   ; INT WS R13 - used for interrupt call (word)
0175      83DC     intwsr14            equ >83dc   ; INT WS R14 - used for interrupt call (word)
0176      83DE     intwsr15            equ >83de   ; INT WS R15 - used for interrupt call (word)
0177      83F6     gplwsr11            equ >83f6   ; GPL WS R11 - return address to interrupt ROM (not used, but overwritten each int)
0178      83F8     gplwsr12            equ >83f8   ; GPL WS R12 - used for cassette test and interrupt hook test (zeroed each int)
0179      83FA     gplwsr13            equ >83fa   ; GPL WS R13 - used in my interrupt handler
0180      83FC     gplwsr14            equ >83fc   ; GPL WS R14 - flags used to detect cassette - must be >0108 (or at least >0020 clear)
0181      83FE     gplwsr15            equ >83fe   ; GPL WS R15 - base address of VDP for status read - must be >8C02

0470               ; Load sprite definitions: Sprite number in R4, CPU data in R0, count of sprites in R5 (MSB)
0471               ; Original: pointer = sprite number, temp = CPU address, a = number sprites
0472               ; Note: sprites are all expected to be double-size 16x16, 32 bytes each, so sprite char 1 is character 4
0473               ; Sprite pattern table at >3800
0474               define_sprite
0475 A1DA C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0476 A1DC C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; Source data.
0477 A1DE C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; VRAM target.
0478 A1E0 0A50  26     sla r0,5            ; sprite number times 32 for bytes
0479 A1E2 0220  22     ai r0,>3800         ; add VDP base
     A1E4 3800     
0480 A1E6 C0C5  18     mov r5,r3		; Length.
0481 A1E8 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make int
0482 A1EA 0A53  26     sla r3,5            ; count times 32
0483 A1EC 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A1EE 0000     
0484 A1F0 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM          ; do the copy
     A1F2 A076     
0485 A1F4 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A1F6 0002     
0486 A1F8 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0487               
0488               ; Load character definitions: Char number in R1, CPU data in R2, count in R3 (MSB)
0489               ; Original: pointer = char number, temp = CPU address, a = number chars
0490               ; Note this loads the pattern three times if in bitmap mode (MODE&0x04)
0491               ; Pattern table at >0000
0492               define_char
0493 A1FA C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0494 A1FC C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; source data
0495 A1FE C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; move input to scratch
0496 A200 0A30  22     sla r0,3            ; char number times 8 (VDP base is 0, so already there)
0497 A202 C0C5  18     mov r5,r3
0498 A204 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make word
0499 A206 0A33  22     sla r3,3            ; count times 8
0500 A208 D160  30     movb @mode,r5       ; get mode flags
     A20A 834E     
0501 A20C 0245  22     andi r5,>0800
     A20E 0800     
0502 A210 1607  14     jne !1              ; not in bitmap mode, do a single copy
0503               
0504 A212 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A214 0000     
0505 A216 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM3         ; do the triple copy
     A218 A090     
0506 A21A 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A21C 0002     
0507 A21E 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0508               
0509               !1
0510 A220 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A222 0000     
0511 A224 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM          ; do the single copy
     A226 A076     
0512 A228 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A22A 0002     
0513 A22C 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0514               
0515               ; Load bitmap color definitions: Char number in R1, CPU data in R2, count in R3 (MSB)
0516               ; Original: pointer = char number, temp = CPU address, a = number chars
0517               ; Note: always does the triple copy. Color table at >2000
0518               define_color
0519 A22E C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0520 A230 C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; source data
0521 A232 C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; move input to scratch
0522 A234 0A30  22     sla r0,3            ; char number times 8
0523 A236 0220  22     ai r0,>2000         ; add base address
     A238 2000     
0524 A23A C0C5  18     mov r5,r3
0525 A23C 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make word
0526 A23E 0A33  22     sla r3,3            ; count times 8
0527 A240 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A242 0000     
0528 A244 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM3         ; do the triple copy
     A246 A090     
0529 A248 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A24A 0002     
0530 A24C 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0531               
0532               ; Update sprite entry - copy data (4 bytes) to sprite table mirror at sprites
0533               ; R4 = sprite number, R5 = byte 1, r6 = byte 2, r7 = byte 3, r0 = byte 4 (all MSB)
0534               ; Original: A = sprite number, source data at sprite_data
0535               update_sprite
0536 A24E 0984  32     srl r4,8            ; make word
0537 A250 0A24  20     sla r4,2            ; x4 for address
0538 A252 0224  22     ai r4,sprites       ; sprite mirror address
     A254 2000     
0539 A256 DD05  32     movb r5,*r4+        ; move bytes
0540 A258 DD06  32     movb r6,*r4+        ; move bytes
0541 A25A DD07  32     movb r7,*r4+        ; move bytes
0542 A25C DD00  32     movb r0,*r4+        ; move bytes
0543 A25E 045B  20     b *r11
0544               
0545               ; SGN R0 - return 1, -1 or 0 as 16 bit
0546               _sgn16
0547 A260 C000  18     mov r0,r0       ; check for zero
0548 A262 1306  14     jeq !1          ; if yes, we're done
0549 A264 0240  22     andi r0,>8000   ; check for negative
     A266 8000     
0550 A268 1302  14     jeq !2          ; was not
0551 A26A 0700  14     seto r0         ; was negative, make it -1
0552 A26C 045B  20     b *r11          ; back to caller
0553               !2
0554 A26E 0580  14     inc r0          ; we know it was zero, and we want 1
0555               !1
0556 A270 045B  20     b *r11          ; back to caller
0557               
0558               ; 16-bit signed modulo. R1 % R2 = R0 - 9900 doesn't do signed divide
0559               ; original was stack%stack=YYAA
0560               ; Remainder is negative if the dividend was negative
0561               _mod16s
0562 A272 04C0  14     clr r0          ; make dividend 32-bit
0563 A274 C082  18     mov r2,r2       ; check divisor for zero
0564 A276 130A  14     jeq !1
0565 A278 0742  18     abs r2          ; make sure divisor is positive
0566 A27A C041  18     mov r1,r1       ; check sign of dividend
0567 A27C 1505  14     jgt !2          ; go do the faster positive version
0568               
0569 A27E 0741  18     abs r1          ; was negative, make it positive
0570 A280 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the division => r2=quotient, r3=remainder
0571 A282 0501  14     neg r1          ; make remainder negative
0572 A284 C001  18     mov r1,r0       ; into r0
0573 A286 045B  20     b *r11
0574               
0575               !2
0576 A288 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the division => r2=quotient, r3=remainder
0577 A28A C001  18     mov r1,r0       ; into r0
0578               !1
0579 A28C 045B  20     b *r11
0580               
0581               ; 16-bit signed divide. R1 / R2 = R0 - 9900 doesn't do signed divide
0582               ; original was stack/stack=YYAA
0583               ; Remainder is negative if the signs differ
0584               _div16s
0585 A28E 04C0  14     clr r0          ; make dividend 32-bit
0586 A290 C0C2  18     mov r2,r3       ; check divisor for zero
0587 A292 1308  14     jeq !1          ;
0588 A294 28C1  18     xor r1,r3
0589 A296 0742  18     abs r2
0590 A298 0741  18     abs r1          ; might as well make them positive now that we have copies
0591 A29A 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the divide => r0=quotient, r1=remainder
0592 A29C 0243  22     andi r3,>8000   ; mask out sign bit
     A29E 8000     
0593 A2A0 1301  14     jeq !1          ; skip ahead to positive version
0594               
0595 A2A2 0500  14     neg r0          ; negate the result
0596               !1
0597 A2A4 045B  20     b *r11
0598               
0599               ; Random number generator - return in R0, (complex one uses R3,R4, simpler one only R0)
0600               ; Original output into YYAA
0601               random
0628               ; simpler one from dreamcast days...

     A2A8 834C

0631 A2AC 1702  14     jnc .rand1          ; jump if no 1

     A2B0 A2B8     
0633               .rand1
0634 A2B2 C800  30     mov r0,@lfsr        ; save the output
     A2B4 834C     
0635 A2B6 045B  20     b *r11
0636               rmask
0637 A2B8 B400         data >b400          ; mask for 16 bit
0639               
0640               ; Set SN Frequency: R0=frequency code, R2=channel command (MSB)
0641               ; Original: A=least significant byte  X=channel command  Y=most significant byte
0642               sn76489_freq
0643 A2BA C0C0  18     mov r0,r3

     A2BE 000F

     A2C6 8400

0649 A2CA 0240  22     andi r0,>003f
     A2CC 003F

0651 A2D0 D800  30     movb r0,@SOUND  ; most significant byte
     A2D2 8400     
0652 A2D4 045B  20     b *r11
0653               
0654               ; Set SN volume: R0=volume (MSB, inverse of attenuation), R2=channel command (MSB)

0656               sn76489_vol

     A2E0 8400

0832               
0833               ; this is where interrupts happen every frame
0834               ; Unlike a normal TI application, this one runs with interrupts ON,
0835               ; so all operations need to be sure to protect VDP address with LIMI 0,
0836               ; as well as any operations that might need to manipulate data managed
0837               ; by this interrupt. We enter via the normal user hook, so WP is on
0838               ; GPLWS, interrupts are off, and the VDP is already reset and status
0839               ; stashed on vdp_status (>837b). Our return address to the ROM is in
0840               ; r11, but we are NOT going to use it so that we don't need to reserve
0841               ; r8 for whatever nonsense it does. That means we need to load intws
0842               ; and RTWP ourselves at the end. We are on our own workspace so we
0843               ; don't have to worry about the main app's workspace.
0844               int_handler
0845               ; first copy the sprite table
0846 A48E 02E0  18     lwpi myintwp        ; separate safe workspace
     A490 8320     
0847               
0849 A492 C820  46     mov @>7ffe,@saved_bank  ; save bank switch page
     A494 7FFE     
     A496 8352     
0851               
0852 A498 020B  20     li r11,>005b        ; >1b00 with the write bit added, and byte flipped
     A49A 005B     
0853 A49C D80B  30     movb r11,@VDPWADR   ; SAL address
     A49E 8C02     
0854 A4A0 06CB  14     swpb r11
0855 A4A2 D80B  30     movb r11,@VDPWADR   ; going to copy the sprite table to VDP
     A4A4 8C02     
0856               
0857 A4A6 D2E0  30     movb @mode,r11
     A4A8 834E     
0858 A4AA 024B  22     andi r11,>0400      ; if bit >04 (inhibit flicker) is cleared, jump ahead to rotate
     A4AC 0400     
0859 A4AE 130A  14     jeq !4
0860               
0861 A4B0 04CB  14     clr r11             ; else we're going to just write it straight across
0862 A4B2 020C  20     li r12,128
     A4B4 0080     
0863 A4B6 020D  20     li r13,sprites
     A4B8 2000     
0864               !7
0865 A4BA D83D  40     movb *r13+,@VDPWDATA
     A4BC 8C00     
0866 A4BE 060C  14     dec r12
0867 A4C0 16FC  14     jne -!7
0868 A4C2 101B  14     jmp !5
0869               
0870               !4
0871 A4C4 D2E0  30     movb @flicker,r11   ; here we write it rotated every frame
     A4C6 834F     
0872 A4C8 022B  22     ai r11,>0400
     A4CA 0400     
0873 A4CC 024B  22     andi r11,>7f00
     A4CE 7F00     
0874 A4D0 D80B  30     movb r11,@flicker
     A4D2 834F     
0875 A4D4 06CB  14     swpb r11            ; make count
0876 A4D6 020C  20     li r12,32           ; count
     A4D8 0020     
0877               
0878               !6
0879 A4DA 022B  22     ai r11,sprites        ; this is still faster than separate incs
     A4DC 2000

0890               ; next read the joysticks - output needs to be 21xxLDRU - 1 and 2 are button and button2 respectively
0891               ; We don't have a button 2. We also need to read the keyboard and fill in key1_data. key2_data we
0892               ; will leave unused. Note key1_data expects Coleco-style 0-9,10-*,11-#,15=not pressed, but we can throw
0893               ; everything else as ASCII. We could do a split keyboard for 2 players, but I guess we'll leave it for now.

     A522 0006

1018               ; given a joystick read in r13, return bits in r12

1929               ; The stack is simulated using R10. It's not used in
1930               ; these functions but the compiled code will need it.
1931               ; To push: dect r10, mov r0,*r10
1932               ; To pop:  mov *r10+,r0
1933               ; However, for JSR a function is helpful - call this like:
1934               ; bl @jsr
1935               ; data <function_address>
1936               jsr
1937 A980 C3BB  30     mov *r11+,r14       ; get the jump address
1938 A982 064A  14     dect r10            ; make room on stack
1939 A984 C68B  30     mov r11,*r10        ; save return address
1940 A986 069E  24     bl *r14             ; new subroutine call, we can come back here
1941 A988 C2FA  30     mov *r10+,r11       ; get real return off stack - warning, all basic functions do this inline rather than return
1942 A98A 045B  20     b *r11              ; back to caller

1984               ;;; CVBasic code starts here
1985               	; 	' ==========================================================================
1986               	; 	' KEYSTONE KAPERS -- CVBasic, dual target TI-99/4A + ColecoVision.
1987               	; 	'
1988               	; 	' Garry Kitchen's 1983 Activision game. See DESIGN.md; 0 records the
1989               	; 	' research and the four places the sources disagree.
1990               	; 	'
1991               	; 	' Fifty seconds to run Harry Hooligan down inside a department store eight
1992               	; 	' screens wide and four levels tall, before he reaches the roof.
1993               	; 	'
1994               	; 	' THE THREE DECISIONS THIS FILE IS BUILT ON, all from DESIGN.md:
1995               	; 	'
1996               	; 	'   * THE VIEW FLIPS, IT DOES NOT SCROLL. Eight discrete screens; crossing
1997               	; 	'     an edge blits the next one. The per-frame budget never pays for the
1998               	; 	'     store at all -- RallyX repaints 576 chars every camera cell and had
1999               	; 	'     to have all its movement rewritten to survive that.
2000               	; 	'   * A SCREEN IS EXACTLY 256 PX, so an actor's x within its screen is one
2001               	; 	'     unsigned byte. No 16-bit world coordinate exists in this program.
2002               	; 	'   * ZERO PER-FRAME VDP READS. An actor's floor is an index into flry(),
2003               	; 	'     never a question asked of the screen, so the Ms. Pac-Man trap
2004               	; 	'     (actors x per-actor search) is absent by construction.
2005               	; 	'
2006               	; 	' The rules that shaped the code, all from CLAUDE.md 3A, because every one
2007               	; 	' of them fails SILENTLY:
2008               	; 	'
2009               	; 	'   * A plain variable is 8-BIT and a CONST over 255 TRUNCATES. Every
2010               	; 	'     name-table offset past row 7 is a #var or a bare literal.
2011               	; 	'   * Every #var comparison is UNSIGNED.
2012               	; 	'   * `<cmp> AND <cmp>` is miscompiled by the 9900 backend. Nested IFs.
2013               	; 	'   * A sprite at y=208 TERMINATES the sprite list. Hidden sprites go 209.
2014               	; 	'   * A GOSUB left by GOTO never pops. Death, catch and escape are STATES
2015               	; 	'     set in a routine and acted on at the top of the main loop.
2016               	; 	'   * MPY clobbers r0. Nothing here multiplies into an index -- the tables
2017               	; 	'     tsrc()/bdst()/lv8() exist precisely so that no multiply is needed on
2018               	; 	'     a path that reads the result back.
2019               	; 	' ==========================================================================
2020               	;
2021               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- BANKING
2022               	; 	' THE ART AND THE STORE MAP LIVE IN ROM BANK 1 ON THE TI. The fixed area
2023               	; 	' is 24,336 bytes -- three 8,112-byte loader pages -- and unbanked this
2024               	; 	' program filled 24,304 of them, so there was no room left for anything at
2025               	; 	' all. `linkticart` does not warn when you exceed it; it silently discards
2026               	; 	' the top of the image, and what goes missing is whatever sits nearest the
2027               	; 	' end, usually a DATA block rather than code. Nothing errors.
2028               	; 	'
2029               	; 	' WHAT IS SAFE TO BANK. Everything moved here is read at SETUP (the
2030               	; 	' DEFINE CHAR / DEFINE SPRITE calls) or on a screen crossing (the template
2031               	; 	' blit and the escalator's phase tables) -- and, because there is exactly
2032               	; 	' ONE data bank and it is selected ONCE at startup and never switched, it
2033               	; 	' stays mapped for the life of the program. The rule in CLAUDE.md 3A is
2034               	; 	' about SWITCHING inside a frame or under the vblank ISR; with a single
2035               	; 	' permanently-selected bank there is no switch to miss. A missed
2036               	; 	' BANK SELECT would return bytes from the wrong page with no error at
2037               	; 	' build or run time, which is why there is only one and it is set before
2038               	; 	' anything reads from it.
2039               	; 	'
2040               	; 	' BANK ROM 128 sizes ColecoVision's Megacart mapper, NOT the TI cart --
2041               	; 	' that comes from how many bank files the assembler emits -- and it is
2042               	; 	' one of only four values the compiler accepts (128/256/512/1024).
2043               	; 	' The whole thing is gated on TI994A: the Coleco build is Z80 and roughly
2044               	; 	' half the size, so it neither needs banking nor wants to become a
2045               	; 	' Megacart image.
2046               	; 	#if TI994A
2047               	; 	BANK ROM 128
2048               	; 	#endif
2049               	; 	#if NES
2050               	; 	' 240 ON THE NES, AND THIS WAS THE FLICKER. There is no sprite-list
2051               	; 	' terminator on that machine -- y is simply a row -- so 209 is a VISIBLE
2052               	; 	' one, and every "hidden" sprite was being drawn in a heap near the bottom
2053               	; 	' of the screen with pattern 0, which is Kelly's hat. Two dozen of them on
2054               	; 	' the same scanlines swamped the eight-per-scanline budget and took the
2055               	; 	' real actors down with them. $F0 is what the prologue's own
2056               	; 	' clear_sprites uses.
2057               	; 	CONST SPRHID = 240
2058               	; 	#else
2059               	; 	CONST SPRHID = 209		' NOT 208 -- 208 terminates the sprite list
2060      00D1     const_SPRHID	equ >00d1
2061               	; 	#endif
2062               	;
2063               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------------- geometry
2064               	; 	' A band is 5 rows: 4 rows of air (32 px) over one floor slab. Standing
2065               	; 	' Kelly is 16 px, so headroom is 16 px and the jump apex is 14 -- two
2066               	; 	' short of the ceiling, because an arc that bonks is silently truncated.
2067               	; 	' 4 px/frame = 240 px/s. At 2 it was not merely sluggish, it was
2068               	; 	' ARITHMETICALLY TOO SLOW: the climb is three traverses = 6,144 px, which
2069               	; 	' at 2 px/frame is 51 seconds of pure running against a 50-second clock,
2070               	; 	' before a single obstacle, escalator ride or catch. At 3 it is 34 s --
2071               	; 	' and 34 s was still wrong, for a reason a per-actor speed check cannot
2072               	; 	' see: HARRY'S CLIMB IS ALSO 34 s (DESIGN.md 4a). Kelly being 1.5x faster
2073               	; 	' bought nothing, because Harry's route is two thirds the length of
2074               	; 	' Kelly's -- he spawns beside floor 2's escalator and effectively skips a
2075               	; 	' traverse. A chase resolves on PATH / SPEED, not on speed, and the two
2076               	; 	' quotients were equal, so pursuit on foot could never close. At 4 the
2077               	; 	' climb is 25 s against Harry's 45, and the elevator buys back more.
2078               	; 	CONST WALKSP = 4		' px per PASS -- the old unit, kept only for
2079      0004     const_WALKSP	equ >0004
2080               	; 					' the checkers' arithmetic and the comments
2081               	; 					' that quote it. Nothing moves by it now.
2082               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS OF A PIXEL PER FRAME, which is what he actually walks by.
2083               	; 	'
2084               	; 	' HIS OLD BEST-CASE SPEED, MADE CONSTANT -- not his old average. WALKSP was
2085               	; 	' 4 px per loop PASS, so what he actually did depended on the screen: 104 px/s
2086               	; 	' on a light one at 26 passes/s, 80 px/s on the lift and escalator screens at
2087               	; 	' 20. Matching the MEASURED AVERAGE of 23.8 passes/s gave 95.6 px/s (102/64),
2088               	; 	' which is the same average and an 8% loss on exactly the screens a chase
2089               	; 	' spends most of its time crossing -- the crook was already per-frame and did
2090               	; 	' not change, so the ratio that decides the chase quietly dropped. Played, it
2091               	; 	' read as only just catching him on the last screen.
2092               	; 	'
2093               	; 	' 111/64 is 104.1 px/s: his best case, everywhere. He is now at least as fast
2094               	; 	' as he ever was on any screen rather than faster on some and slower on
2095               	; 	' others, and the chase margin goes from 10.6 s to 17.3 s.
2096               	; 	CONST KWALK64 = 111
2097      006F     const_KWALK64	equ >006f
2098               	; 	' The bounce phase, in sixty-fourths of a phase per frame. 32 phases at
2099               	; 	' 25/64 per frame is 1.37 s an arc, against the 1.35 s one phase per pass
2100               	; 	' gives at 23.8 passes a second.
2101               	; 	CONST BOUNCE64 = 25
2102      0019     const_BOUNCE64	equ >0019
2103               	; 	CONST XWALL = 232		' furthest left edge at the store's east wall
2104      00E8     const_XWALL	equ >00e8
2105               	; 	' AND THE ROOF HAS NO EAST WALL, so the crook runs two characters further.
2106               	; 	' Floors 1-3 end in an ENDWALL character at column 31 and XWALL stops an
2107               	; 	' actor just short of it. The roof does not have one -- its east end is the
2108               	; 	' edge of the BUILDING, the skyline carries on to the screen edge, and the
2109               	; 	' round ends with him going over it.
2110               	; 	'
2111               	; 	' 252 IS FOUR PIXELS SHORT OF THE LAST COLUMN, and that is the point: his
2112               	; 	' sprite is 16 px wide, so at 240 he stands flush against the edge FULLY
2113               	; 	' VISIBLE and then simply stops existing -- `do_escape` runs `hide_all` on
2114               	; 	' the same pass. At 252 twelve of those sixteen pixels are already clipped
2115               	; 	' off the screen when he goes, so he reads as having walked off the roof
2116               	; 	' rather than having been deleted from it. The arrival test allows 6 px of
2117               	; 	' slack, so the last frame he is drawn on shows between one and four
2118               	; 	' columns of him.
2119               	; 	'
2120               	; 	' 255 is the true ceiling and buys three more pixels; 252 keeps a little
2121               	; 	' headroom for an off-by-one in whatever edits this next.
2122               	; 	'
2123               	; 	' This is only reachable because the EXIT DOOR that stood at columns 28-30
2124               	; 	' was removed (genstore.py, the roof's east template). Six cells of white
2125               	; 	' box on dark blue, reading on screen as purple dots -- it was asked about
2126               	; 	' as a graphical fault, it says he leaves through a doorway rather than off
2127               	; 	' a roof, and it was exactly where he used to stop.
2128               	; 	CONST XROOF = 252
2129      00FC     const_XROOF	equ >00fc
2130               	; 	CONST XWALW = 8			' nearest left edge at the west wall
2131      0008     const_XWALW	equ >0008
2132               	; 	CONST STANDH = 24		' Kelly standing -- TWO SPRITES tall
2133      0018     const_STANDH	equ >0018
2134               	; 	CONST JUMPTUCK = 2		' run-2 jump pose ends two rows above run-1 feet
2135      0002     const_JUMPTUCK	equ >0002
2136               	; 	' KELLY DUCKED. It was 8 px, which is not a crouch -- it is a squash, with
2137               	; 	' no room to draw a figure bending in a DIRECTION. 11 px is, and the
2138               	; 	' biplane is raised to match (obh below, and the hitbox in coll_obst):
2139               	; 	' with the plane at 16..22 an 11 px crouch passes five pixels under it and
2140               	; 	' a 24 px standing Kop does not. The apex is 14, so a jump still cannot
2141               	; 	' clear it either -- the plane stays the one obstacle that must be ducked.
2142               	; 	'
2143               	; 	' AND 11 IS THE CEILING, not a preference. Duckable means the obstacle
2144               	; 	' clears the crouch, jumpable means it clears under the apex; raising the
2145               	; 	' crouch raises the duckable floor, so past 11 a band of beach-ball
2146               	; 	' heights is neither. A sweep of every crouch height against every ball
2147               	; 	' hitbox puts the limit at 11, and shrinking the ball does not move it --
2148               	; 	' the apex is what binds. assets/checkball.py fails the build on it.
2149               	; 	CONST DUCKH = 11		' Kelly ducked -- what he COLLIDES as
2150      000B     const_DUCKH	equ >000b
2151               	; 	' AND WHAT HE IS DRAWN AS, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME NUMBER YET.
2152               	; 	'
2153               	; 	' The crouch was redrawn with the head and hat at FULL SIZE on top of a
2154               	; 	' squatting body, which is what the reference does -- and the standing head
2155               	; 	' alone is 11 px, the whole of DUCKH. The figure is 16.
2156               	; 	'
2157               	; 	' These two must converge and today they do not, so a ball between 11 and
2158               	; 	' 16 px passes through his hat without hitting him. That is a visible lie
2159               	; 	' and it is deliberate for now: with one constant the crouch would instead

2587               	; 	' TWO SECONDS BETWEEN FLOORS. `elt` counts down by `fdv`, the FRAME
2588               	; 	' delta, so this is real frames and not loop passes -- 120 of them is
2589               	; 	' 2.0 s on both 60 Hz targets, and it stays 2.0 s when the loop gets
2590               	; 	' busy. It was 45 (0.75 s), which is faster than a lift has any business
2591               	; 	' being and gave the doors barely time to read as opening.
2592               	; 	CONST ELMOVE = 120		' frames in transit between floors
2593      0078     const_ELMOVE	equ >0078
2594               	; 	' HOW FAR THE SECOND HAZARD ON A FLOOR TRAILS THE FIRST, in pixels.
2595               	; 	'
2596               	; 	' THERE ARE ONLY TWO SAFE ANSWERS. Kelly closes on an oncoming hazard at
2597               	; 	' (KWALK64 + its speed)/64 px a FRAME -- 2.53 at the slow speed, 2.92 at
2598               	; 	' the fast one -- and the jump arc holds its apex for 9 frames and is
2599               	; 	' airborne for 28. So:
2600               	; 	'
2601               	; 	'   <= 22 px   ONE JUMP CLEARS BOTH -- the pair drifts under the apex
2602               	; 	'   >= 82 px   he can LAND BETWEEN them -- a whole jump fits in the gap
2603               	; 	'
2604               	; 	' Anything in between is the dangerous middle: too far to clear together,
2605               	; 	' too close to land between. The gap shipped at 46 px west of the lift and
2606               	; 	' 70 px east of it -- 46 is inside the first window and 70 is squarely in
2607               	; 	' that middle, which is the asymmetry that got reported. It then shipped at
2608               	; 	' 20, in the first window, which is a pair taken as ONE obstacle.
2609               	; 	'
2610               	; 	' 104 IS MEASURED FROM THE ORIGINAL, not chosen. A frame-by-frame census of
2611               	; 	' a full 2600 playthrough (assets/ref2600/hazards.md) finds that two moving
2612               	; 	' hazards on one floor are NEVER closer than 108 px in our scale -- not once
2613               	; 	' in 21 levels -- and that its static radios come as close as 54. Our own
2614               	; 	' arc independently puts the land-between threshold at 82 px for a mover and
2615               	; 	' 49 for a static one, so the original sits just above both, from evidence
2616               	; 	' that knows nothing about this jump. That is the run / jump / run / jump
2617               	; 	' the reviewer described, and it is what the 20 px pair was not.
2618               	; 	'
2619               	; 	' THE PRICE IS SLOT 0's JITTER, and it is arithmetic, not a choice. `stag`
2620               	; 	' is distance from the FAR edge, so the second hazard sits GAP px nearer the
2621               	; 	' wall the player walks in through. He needs a reaction budget there
2622               	; 	' (checkspace.py's WARNPX, 120 px), and 120 + 104 = 224 of the 240 px of
2623               	; 	' placeable floor -- so the pair can only slide 16 px. Hence HAZMASK below.
2624               	; 	' That is not less faithful than what it replaces: the original places its
2625               	; 	' radios on exactly THREE fixed positions per floor, so it has no jitter at
2626               	; 	' all. assets/checkspace.py checks the gap, the entry distance and the
2627               	; 	' offset rule together, and checkspace_test.py proves it still rejects 70
2628               	; 	' and 176 -- and now 71, which only the FASTEST hazard can see.
2629               	; 	CONST HAZGAP = 104
2630      0068     const_HAZGAP	equ >0068
2631               	; 	' Slot 0's stagger mask ONCE A FLOOR CAN CARRY TWO. Before that a floor has
2632               	; 	' one hazard, the pair arithmetic above does not apply, and slot 0 keeps its
2633               	; 	' full 64 px of jitter -- which is most of the early game, where the player
2634               	; 	' meets the fewest hazards and variety is worth the most.
2635               	; 	CONST HAZMASK = 15
2636      000F     const_HAZMASK	equ >000f

2641               	; 					' built from other CONSTs is exactly the
2642               	; 					' folded-constant trap in CLAUDE.md 3A
2643               	;
2644               	; 	' escalator boarding zones, in CENTRE-x pixels
2645               	; 	' ESCALATOR BOARDING ZONES, IN PIXELS, AND THEY TRACK THE ART.
2646               	; 	' The flight is drawn as four rows of two characters stepping two columns
2647               	; 	' per row: west runs cols 1-2 (top) down to 7-8 (foot), east runs 29-30
2648               	; 	' (top) down to 23-24 (foot). These zones ARE those columns x8. When the
2649               	; 	' escalator art changed from a filled triangle to a stepped flight the
2650               	; 	' foot moved, and a boarding zone left where it was would put the player
2651               	; 	' on a staircase that is not under them -- no error, just a floor that
2652               	; 	' teleports you when you walk over an empty patch of it.
2653               	; 	' THESE ARE THE DRAWN STEPS, in screen pixels. The flight is fifteen
2654               	; 	' characters wide: its foot tread sits at x 95-103 (west) and 152-160
2655               	; 	' (east), its head tread at 23-31 and 224-232. An actor rides between
2656               	; 	' those, so the numbers here are the ART's, and moving the art without
2657               	; 	' moving them puts the rider beside the escalator rather than on it.
2658               	; 	' THE RIDER STANDS ON A STEP, and everything about the ride follows from
2659               	; 	' WHICH ONE. The staircase is a straight line -- a step 4 px higher is 8
2660               	; 	' px further along it -- so one number, the step's height above the floor
2661               	; 	' being left, fixes both the rider's x and the rest of the ride:
2662               	; 	'
2663               	; 	'     west  klx = 99 - 2*height        east  klx = 140 + 2*height
2664               	; 	'
2665               	; 	' The bottom step is 4 px up, so a rider walking on boards at klx = 91
2666               	; 	' (west) or 148 (east); the head step is 40 up, so the ride ends at 19 or
2667               	; 	' 220. Those are the ART's numbers -- the foot tread is drawn at x 95-103
2668               	; 	' west and 152-160 east, the head tread at 23-31 and 224-232 -- so moving
2669               	; 	' the art without moving these puts the rider beside the staircase.
2670               	; 	'
2671               	; 	' THE PHASE MATTERS. The steps climb 1 px a frame and the animation runs
2672               	; 	' four 1 px phases, so the bottom step is 4 + escp px up, not 4. Boarding
2673               	; 	' without that term leaves the feet up to 3 px out of register with the
2674               	; 	' tread and the whole ride drifts, which is exactly what "he floats
2675               	; 	' beside the steps" looked like.
2676               	; 	CONST ESCFX = 91		' west foot: rider's x when boarding
2677      005B     const_ESCFX	equ >005b
2678               	; 	CONST ESCFXE = 148		' east foot
2679      0094     const_ESCFXE	equ >0094
2680               	; 	CONST ESCHX = 19		' west head: rider's x on arrival
2681      0013     const_ESCHX	equ >0013
2682               	; 	CONST ESCHXE = 220		' east head
2683      00DC     const_ESCHXE	equ >00dc
2684               	; 	CONST ESCRISE = 40		' floor to floor, and the ride's length
2685      0028     const_ESCRISE	equ >0028
2686               	;
2687               	; 	' TIMER UNITS PER KROOK, AND A UNIT IS NOT A SECOND. Measured off the
2688               	; 	' reference video (DESIGN.md 0m): the original counts 50 down to 0 and a
2689               	; 	' unit lasts 1.99 s, so a round is about 100 seconds. TICKFR below is
2690               	; 	' what makes it so here.
2691               	; 	CONST TIMEL = 50		' timer units per Krook
2692      0032     const_TIMEL	equ >0032
2693               	; 	' FRAMES PER TIMER UNIT. 120, not 60, and this is not cosmetic -- it is
2694               	; 	' what makes a round finishable. Everything that MOVES in this game is
2695               	; 	' paced per loop PASS, and the loop runs about 25 passes a second, so
2696               	; 	' Kelly's 4 px a pass is ~100 px/s (the reference's Kelly is 102, so the
2697               	; 	' speeds match). The timer, though, is paced by the frame DELTA -- real
2698               	; 	' wall-clock time. At 60 frames a unit the round was 50 real seconds
2699               	; 	' while Kelly's route to the roof takes about 72, so the clock ran out
2700               	; 	' before either of them could get there and every round ended on a
2701               	; 	' timeout. checkchase.py hid it by assuming 60 passes a second; it now
2702               	; 	' models the real rate.
2703               	; 	CONST TICKFR = 120
2704      0078     const_TICKFR	equ >0078
2705               	; 	' NINE TIMER UNITS -- not ten, and not nine seconds. Every source says a
2706               	; 	' cart, ball or radio costs "9 seconds", and what they mean is the number
2707               	; 	' on the HUD, because that is what the manual calls seconds. So the
2708               	; 	' DISPLAYED count drops by 9. A unit is about two real seconds
2709               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 0m), which makes one careless cart cost roughly eighteen --
2710               	; 	' close to a fifth of the round, and the reason the refractory latch
2711               	; 	' below matters so much.
2712               	; 	CONST HITPEN = 9		' timer units a cart / ball / radio costs
2713      0009     const_HITPEN	equ >0009
2714               	; 	' HOW LONG A HIT SOUNDS, IN LOOP PASSES -- and therefore how long the
2715               	; 	' store stands still for one. The two are the same number on purpose:
2716               	; 	' the freeze is meant to last exactly as long as the noise, so a change
2717               	; 	' to one that did not move the other would leave either a silent pause
2718               	; 	' or a sound playing over a resumed game. Passes, not frames, because
2719               	; 	' both counters are spent once per pass in sfx_tick and the main loop.
2720               	; 	CONST HITSND = 20
2721      0014     const_HITSND	equ >0014
2722               	; 	CONST HITREF = 45		' frames before the SAME obstacle can charge
2723      002D     const_HITREF	equ >002d
2724               	; 					' again. See coll_obst -- clearing the latch
2725               	; 					' on the first non-overlapping frame is not
2726               	; 					' enough, because a bouncing ball leaves
2727               	; 					' contact between bounces.
2728               	;
2729               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- tables
2730               	; 	DIM flry(4)			' floor surface y, by level
2731               	; 	DIM #bdst(4)			' band name-table offset, by level
2732               	; 	DIM #tsrc(15)			' template source offset, by template id
2733               	; 	' THE NES CANNOT READ ITS OWN VIDEO MEMORY BACK, so anything this
2734               	; 	' program does as read-modify-write needs the "read" to come from RAM
2735               	; 	' instead. WRTVRM on that target does not touch the PPU at all -- it
2736               	; 	' queues into PPUBUF for the NMI to flush -- so a read would be both
2737               	; 	' illegal during rendering and blind to everything still in the queue.
2738               	; 	'
2739               	; 	' The radar is the only read-modify-write on the PATTERN table: it ORs
2740               	; 	' pixel rows into its canvas characters, 208-255, eight bytes each.
2741               	; 	' 384 bytes of the NES's 1,227 free, and nothing on the other targets.
2742               	; 	#if NES
2743               	; 	DIM nsc(768)			' radar canvas pattern shadow, 48 tiles x 16
2744               	; 	DIM nesb(96)			' the escalator's six characters, staged for the NMI
2745               	; 	DIM nmsg(4)			' packed surrounding attribute halves for GAME OVER
2746               	; 	#endif
2747               	; 	DIM lv8(4)			' lv*8, so no multiply lands on an index
2748               	; 	DIM rhaz(16)			' packed hazard map, retained across deaths
2749               	; 	DIM jarc(32)			' the jump arc: 30 frames, apex 14
2750               	; 	DIM msk(8)
2751               	;
2752               	; 	' EIGHT obstacle slots -- TWO per band, and that number is forced.
2753               	; 	'
2754               	; 	' The VDP shows four sprites per scanline and DROPS the rest by slot
2755               	; 	' order; it does not flicker them, they simply are not there. Three per
2756               	; 	' band was sized against Kelly alone (1 + 3 = 4) and forgot that HARRY
2757               	; 	' can be on that band too -- and when he is, the fifth sprite on his
2758               	; 	' scanline is the highest-numbered obstacle, which vanishes while still
2759               	; 	' being solid. An invisible thing that costs nine seconds is the worst
2760               	; 	' failure in the game and it only happens when the crook is next to you,
2761               	; 	' which is exactly when you are not looking at the floor.
2762               	; 	'
2763               	; 	' Kelly (slot 0) + Harry (slot 1) + two obstacles = four. Provably never
2764               	; 	' dropped, on any band, in any situation.
2765               	; 	'
2766               	; 	' ...AND THAT CAP IS ABOUT SPRITES, WHICH A RADIO IS NOT. The scanline
2767               	; 	' limit is the whole argument above, and it does not reach the radio: a
2768               	; 	' radio is four CHARACTERS stamped into the name table by draw_radios, it
2769               	; 	' costs no sprite, and the VDP will happily draw a hundred of them on one
2770               	; 	' line. The original puts up to THREE on a floor (assets/ref2600/hazards.md
2771               	; 	' measures them at three fixed positions), and the reason we had two was
2772               	; 	' this comment being read as a limit on hazards when it is a limit on
2773               	; 	' sprites.
2774               	; 	'
2775               	; 	' So there are TWELVE slots in two groups, and the split is deliberate:
2776               	; 	'
2777               	; 	'   0-7    two per band, band*2 + slot -- ANY kind, and these are the ones
2778               	; 	'          that own sprites 8-15 (propellers 16-23). Untouched.
2779               	; 	'   8-11   ONE per band, 8 + band -- RADIO OR EMPTY, never a sprite.
2780               	; 	'
2781               	; 	' Keeping the new slots in their own block rather than making the stride
2782               	; 	' three is what leaves draw_obst's `FOR di = 0 TO 7` and its `ds = di + 8`
2783               	; 	' exactly as they were. A stride of three would have scattered the
2784               	; 	' sprite-bearing slots to 0,1,3,4,6,7,9,10 and every sprite number in the
2785               	; 	' game would have had to be recomputed -- to place a thing that does not
2786               	; 	' use one.
2787               	; 	DIM obk(12)			' kind, 0 = empty
2788               	; 	DIM obx(12)			' x within the screen
2789               	; 	DIM obd(12)			' 0 = moving left, 1 = right
2790               	; 	DIM obh(12)			' art-bottom height above the slab
2791               	; 	DIM obc(12)			' cell column, radios only -- they are chars
2792               	; 	DIM obp(12)			' bounce phase, balls only
2793               	; 	DIM obht(12)			' hit refractory, per obstacle -- see coll_obst
2794               	;
2795               	; 	DIM cok(4)			' this screen's collectible, per band
2796               	; 	DIM coc(4)			' its column
2797               	; 	DIM takn(4)			' 32 bits: which bands have been cleaned out
2798               	;
2799               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- state
2800               	; 	' Kelly
2801               	; 	' klv 0..3 (0 = floor 1, 3 = roof), klsc 0..7, klx 0..255
2802               	; 	' Harry the same. NOTHING in this program is a world coordinate.
2803               	;
2804               	; 	' EVERYTHING IS BUILT BEFORE THE TITLE IS DRAWN, NOT BEHIND IT.
2805               	; 	'
2806               	; 	' The opposite order was tried first, on the reasoning that only the font
2807               	; 	' is needed to put text on a screen: draw the title immediately, then
2808               	; 	' define the store characters, the store colours, the escalator deck, the
2809               	; 	' radar canvas and eight sprite sets while the player reads it. None of
2810               	; 	' that is touched until new_game, so nothing was out of order.
2811               	; 	'
2812               	; 	' IT MADE THE TITLE APPEAR SOONER AND ARRIVE DEAD. A third of a second of
2813               	; 	' a finished screen that was not yet reading the keyboard -- long enough to
2814               	; 	' swallow the first digit of 8-3-8, and reported as a start press that did
2815               	; 	' not take. A menu the player cannot act on is not up yet, whatever is
2816               	; 	' painted on it.
2817               	; 	'
2818               	; 	' So the work moved back in front. The screen appears later and is live on
2819               	; 	' the frame it appears, and the prompt printed on it is honest rather than
2820               	; 	' hopeful. The cost lands once, on a black screen at power-on, where there
2821               	; 	' is nothing to act on anyway.
2822               	; 	'
2823               	; 	' And it stays once: `GOTO boot` after a game over re-enters BELOW this, so
2824               	; 	' a second game reaches its title in a single redraw.
2825               	; 	GOSUB setup_font
2826 A9FA 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     A9FC A980     
2827 A9FE AB8E     	data cvb_SETUP_FONT

2829 AA00 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     AA02 A980     
2830 AA04 AC3A     	data cvb_SETUP_REST

2832 AA06 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     AA08 A980

2835               	; boot:
2836               cvb_BOOT
2837               	; 	' Coming back from a game over the store is still on screen, so the title
2838               	; 	' has to be redrawn; the first time through, this is its first draw.
2839               	; 	GOSUB title_draw
2840 AA0C 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     AA0E A980     
2841 AA10 AFA0     	data cvb_TITLE_DRAW
2842               	; 	GOSUB title_input
2843 AA12 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     AA14 A980     
2844 AA16 B09C     	data cvb_TITLE_INPUT
2845               	; 	' LET GO OF FIRE BEFORE PLAY BEGINS.
2846               	; 	'
2847               	; 	' title_input returns ON the press, so the button is still down when the
2848               	; 	' round starts and read_input sees it on the very first pass. jrel is
2849               	; 	' supposed to absorb that -- start_krook clears it, so the latch demands a
2850               	; 	' release before the first jump -- and in play it did not, reported twice.
2851               	; 	' Rather than keep reasoning about the order of two latches, this waits
2852               	; 	' for the thing itself: the key that said "start" is not in the buffer any
2853               	; 	' more when the loop begins.
2854               	; 	'
2855               	; 	' CAPPED AT A SECOND, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE COUNTER. A stuck
2856               	; 	' or shorted fire line would otherwise hang the game on a black screen for
2857               	; 	' ever, which is exactly the mistake the ALPHA LOCK check made in its first
2858               	; 	' version -- refusing to start until a condition cleared that never would.
2859               	; 	' A survivable input quirk must not become a dead game, so after sixty
2860               	; 	' frames it gives up and plays anyway.
2861               	; 	brw = 0
2862 AA18 04C0  14 	clr r0
2863 AA1A D800  38 	movb r0,@cvb_BRW
     AA1C 20B7     
2864               	; btn_rel:
2865               cvb_BTN_REL
2866               	; 	WAIT
2867 AA1E 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     AA20 A980     
2868 AA22 A656     	data wait
2869               	; 	brw = brw + 1

2926               	; 	' MATCH THE TI'S LOOP RATE, AND DO IT HERE RATHER THAN ANYWHERE ELSE.
2927               	; 	'
2928               	; 	' Three things in this game are paced per LOOP PASS and must stay locked to
2929               	; 	' one another: the escalator's four-phase step animation, Kelly riding it
2930               	; 	' and Harry riding it. CLAUDE.md 3A is explicit that a cyclic animation can
2931               	; 	' only be stepped by ONE phase per pass -- step it by two and the direction
2932               	; 	' becomes unreadable, by three and the staircase visibly runs backwards --
2933               	; 	' so the riders have to be on the pass clock too, and changing any ONE of
2934               	; 	' the three decouples a rider from the tread he is standing on.
2935               	; 	'
2936               	; 	' The NES and Coleco builds run more passes per second than the TI, so the
2937               	; 	' escalator ran at that rate: correct, coupled, and far too fast. The only
2938               	; 	' change that keeps all three together is to the LOOP RATE itself. The TI
2939               	; 	' measures ~24 passes a second (CLAUDE.md 3A: 2,335 passes over ~98 s), so
2940               	; 	' a pass is 2.5 frames, and `nespw` alternates 2 and 3 to average it.
2941               	; 	'
2942               	; 	' IT IS A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING. A pass that already took longer than nespw
2943               	; 	' frames waits for nothing, so a heavy screen still runs at whatever rate
2944               	; 	' it can -- exactly as on the TI.
2945               	; nes_pace:
2946               	; 	#fd = FRAME - #lf
2947               	; 	IF #fd < nespw THEN
2948               	; 		WAIT
2949               	; 		GOTO nes_pace
2950               	; 	END IF

3210               	;
3211               	; 	#if NES
3212               	; 	' THE NES'S TWO STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCES, SETTLED ONCE, HERE.
3213               	; 	'
3214               	; 	' 1. WHERE THE PATTERNS LIVE. In 8x16 sprite mode the sprite pattern table
3215               	; 	'    is chosen by bit 0 of each OAM tile byte and the PPUCTRL bit is
3216               	; 	'    ignored -- and every pattern number in this game is a multiple of
3217               	; 	'    four, so that bit is always 0 and the sprites are nailed to $0000.
3218               	; 	'    nes_bgbank therefore moves the BACKGROUND to $1000 rather than trying
3219               	; 	'    to move the sprites, which also lands the background patterns at
3220               	; 	'    address 4096, exactly where the TMS bitmap mode's third screen third
3221               	; 	'    had them -- so the radar's pattern writes need a stride and nothing
3222               	; 	'    else.
3223               	; 	'
3224               	; 	' 2. COLOUR DOES NOT MAP AND IS NOT PRETENDED TO. The NES colours in 16x16
3225               	; 	'    attribute blocks; this game colours per character, two colours a
3226               	; 	'    cell. So the store is drawn in ONE ink and the actors get four
3227               	; 	'    palettes, picked by the low two bits of the colour argument the
3228               	; 	'    SPRITE statements already pass -- 1 (black) -> dark grey, 4/8 (blue)
3229               	; 	'    -> blue, 14 (grey) -> grey, 11/15 (skin, white) -> white. Nothing in
3230               	; 	'    the game source has to know.
3231               	; 	ASM JSR nes_bgbank
3232               	; 	ASM JSR nes_apuon
3233               	;
3234               	; 	' Grey is shared index 0 during gameplay. Other indices are per region.
3235               	; 	' gennescolor.py assigns P3 only to counter quadrants, retaining green
3236               	; 	' wall and gold floor colours. Fixtures with black outlines use P0.
3237               	; 	PALETTE 1,26			' P0: green, black, gold
3238               	; 	PALETTE 2,15			' black escalators and fixture outlines
3239               	; 	PALETTE 3,40
3240               	; 	PALETTE 5,1			' P1 HUD/upper skyline: blue, pink, gold
3241               	; 	PALETTE 6,36
3242               	; 	PALETTE 7,40
3243               	; 	PALETTE 9,38			' P2 lower skyline: orange, black, gold
3244               	; 	PALETTE 10,1			' unused skyline index 2: navy message bottom border
3245               	; 	PALETTE 11,40
3246               	; 	PALETTE 13,26			' P3 counters: green, blue, gold
3247               	; 	PALETTE 14,1			' same navy in counter quadrants
3248               	; 	PALETTE 15,40
3249               	;
3250               	; 	' AND FOUR FOR THE ACTORS, which DO get one each because a sprite carries
3251               	; 	' its own palette number. nes_spal maps the TMS colour every SPRITE
3252               	; 	' statement already passes onto these four.
3253               	; 	PALETTE 17,18			' 0 -- blue   Kelly's trousers
3254               	; 	PALETTE 21,15			' 1 -- black  hats, Harry's stripes, the Kop's dot.
3255               	; 					' FIFTEEN, NOT ZERO: on this palette $0F is
3256               	; 					' black and $00 is a dark GREY, so every hat
3257               	; 					' and every stripe was coming out grey.
3258               	; 	PALETTE 22,23			' black sprite palette, index 2: brown suitcase outline
3259               	; 	PALETTE 25,39			' 2 -- skin   faces and the biplane
3260               	; 	PALETTE 26,16			' 2 colour 2 -- GREY, the lift car on the radar
3261               	; 	' AND THE BALL IS RED, which it already is on the TI: C_BALL is TMS 8,
3262               	; 	' medium red. nes_spal sends that to sprite palette 2, and palette 2's
3263               	; 	' colour ONE is the skin tone -- so on this machine the ball came out the
3264               	; 	' same pale orange as a face.
3265               	; 	'
3266               	; 	' A sprite here is ONE bitplane, so its pixels are whichever index the
3267               	; 	' upload writes and the OAM byte only chooses the palette. The lift car on
3268               	; 	' the radar already solved this: it is uploaded with `nink = 2` and reads
3269               	; 	' palette 2's second entry. The ball does the same with the THIRD, which
3270               	; 	' nothing else uses.
3271               	; 	PALETTE 27,22			' 2 colour 3 -- RED, the bouncing balls
3272               	; 	PALETTE 29,48			' 3 -- white  Harry, the carts, the lift car
3273               	;
3274               	; 	#endif
3275               	; 	#if TI994A
3276               	; 	#else
3277               	; 	nespw = 2			' NES/Coleco start on a 2-frame pass
3278               	; 	#endif
3279               	;
3280               	; 	' THE ONE AND ONLY BANK SWITCH THE PROGRAM EVER MAKES, and it happens
3281               	; 	' here, before the first frame.
3282               	; 	'
3283               	; 	' There are two data banks now. Bank 1 holds everything read while the
3284               	; 	' game is running -- sprite and store art, the templates, the lookup
3285               	; 	' tables -- and it is selected at the end of this routine and never
3286               	; 	' changed again, so every VARPTR/PEEK read in the program is reading a
3287               	; 	' page that is permanently mapped. That is the property that makes
3288               	; 	' banking safe here: a missed BANK SELECT returns bytes from the wrong
3289               	; 	' page with no error at build or run time, so the safest number of
3290               	; 	' switches during play is none.
3291               	; 	'
3292               	; 	' Bank 2 exists to hold data that is read ONCE, at setup, and never
3293               	; 	' again. The font is exactly that: two DEFINEs copy it into VRAM and
3294               	; 	' nothing reads font_bits or font_col for the rest of the run. So it can
3295               	; 	' live on a page that is mapped for the length of those two statements.
3296               	; 	'
3297               	; 	' IF THIS EVER FAILS IT FAILS LOUDLY. Select the wrong bank here and the
3298               	; 	' font is garbage on the title screen, immediately and unmistakably --
3299               	; 	' which is the same diagnostic the font used to provide by staying out of
3300               	; 	' the banks altogether, recovered for free.
3301               	; 	#if TI994A
3302               	; 	BANK SELECT 2
3303 ABB4 04E0  34 	clr @>6008
     ABB6 6008     
3304               	; 	#endif
3305               	;
3306               	; 	#if NES
3307               	; 	' THE FONT IS SENT WITH A COLOUR TABLE SO ITS PAPER IS NOT THE BACKDROP.
3308               	; 	'
3309               	; 	' With `#ncol = 0` the uploader puts ink `nink` on index 0 -- the UNIVERSAL
3310               	; 	' backdrop, black in the game -- so every character of text sat in its own
3311               	; 	' black box. The score line was a black strip across the top of a blue sky.
3312               	; 	'
3313               	; 	' Index 0 cannot be set per region (it is one colour for the whole screen),
3314               	; 	' so the only way to give text a ground is to put its PAPER on another
3315               	; 	' index, and paper is written into the second bitplane when the character
3316               	; 	' is uploaded. Hence a table: $B4 is light yellow on dark blue, which
3317               	; 	' nes_inkmap sends to index 3 and index 1.
3318               	; 	'
3319               	; 	' ONE FONT, NOT TWO. The first attempt at this made a SECOND copy of the
3320               	; 	' font at codes 197.. so the HUD could differ from the message boxes, and
3321               	; 	' that was both unnecessary and impossible: in game the HUD and the boxes
3322               	; 	' are the same text and want the same treatment, and 197..207 is only
3323               	; 	' ELEVEN free codes -- 208 up is the radar canvas (genart's SCAN_FIRST),
3324               	; 	' which scan_wipe rewrites as raw pattern memory every frame. The 59-char
3325               	; 	' copy appeared to upload and was scribbled over from its twelfth character
3326               	; 	' on. See checkpat.py, which now knows the canvas owns those codes.
3327               	; 	'
3328               	; 	' What index 1 IS comes from the attribute table, per region: the HUD row
3329               	; 	' is on P1 (dark blue, below) and the store is on P0.
3330               	; 	#nsrc = VARPTR font_bits(0)
3331               	; 	nchr = 32
3332               	; 	ncnt = 59
3333               	; 	ntab = 1
3334               	; 	#ncol = VARPTR nes_fcol(0)
3335               	; 	nink = 3
3336               	; 	GOSUB nes_def
3337               	; 	#else
3338               	; 	DEFINE CHAR 32,59,font_bits
3339 ABB8 0204  20 	li r4,32
     ABBA 0020     
3340 ABBC 0205  20 	li r5,15104
     ABBE 3B00     
3341 ABC0 0200  20 	li r0,cvb_FONT_BITS
     ABC2 672A     
3342 ABC4 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     ABC6 A980     
3343 ABC8 A1FA     	data define_char
3344               	; 	#endif
3345               	; 	' Without this the font keeps whatever CVBasic left in the colour table --
3346               	; 	' white on transparent -- which over a green store made the HUD unreadable.
3347               	; 	'
3348               	; 	' THIS WAS A VPOKE LOOP AND IT WAS THE SLOWEST THING IN THE BOOT: 1,416
3349               	; 	' writes of one constant, paced by 24 WAITs, which is what made the title
3350               	; 	' fill in visibly instead of appearing. DEFINE COLOR does the same job in a
3351               	; 	' single call with interrupts off, and it writes all three screen thirds
3352               	; 	' itself -- define_color always takes the LDIRVM3 triple-copy path, which is
3353               	; 	' also why esc_deck_col and floor0_colour below CANNOT use it: they patch
3354               	; 	' one third each.
3355               	; 	'
3356               	; 	' The table is 472 identical bytes (genfont.py emits it beside the glyphs).
3357               	; 	' It reads as waste and is not: it lives in the data bank, which had 860
3358               	; 	' bytes spare, while the loop it replaced cost time in the one place the
3359               	; 	' player is made to wait.
3360               	; 	#if NES
3361               	; 	' no colour table on this machine -- see nes_setup
3362               	; 	#else

3377               	; 	'

3928               	; 	' THE JUMP ARC IS A TABLE, not integration. That makes the 14 px apex a
3929               	; 	' property of the data rather than of a fixed-point velocity that has to
3930               	; 	' be tuned, and it keeps every comparison in the jump 8-bit and unsigned.
3931               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a depends on the apex being exactly 14.
3932               	; 	'
3933               	; 	' THIRTY FRAMES WITH NINE OF THEM AT THE APEX. The first version was 24
3934               	; 	' frames that touched 14 for only four, which made every jump a timing
3935               	; 	' test rather than a decision -- you had to leave the ground on exactly
3936               	; 	' the right frame or clip the thing you were jumping. Widening the
3937               	; 	' plateau rather than raising the apex keeps the ball arithmetic in
3938               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a intact (the apex is what that depends on) while making the
3939               	; 	' window forgiving: the player still has to CHOOSE to jump, but no longer
3940               	; 	' has to be frame-perfect about it.
3941               	; 	' THE ARC IS A TABLE, not thirty assignments -- each of those compiled to
3942               	; 	' several bytes of code, and the fixed area is the binding budget.

4003 AEF0 C03A  30 	mov *r10+,r0

4005               	;
4006               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR TABLE WAS 472 BYTES OF ONE REPEATED VALUE, which is a
4007               	; 	' fifth of what the fixed area had left. DEFINE COLOR copies such a table
4008               	; 	' out of ROM into all three screen thirds; writing the constant straight
4009               	; 	' into the colour table does the same job for the price of a loop, and
4010               	; 	' the loop runs once, at boot.
4011               	; 	'
4012               	; 	' The colour table is at >2000 and the VDP mirrors it once per screen
4013               	; 	' third, >800 apart. Both numbers were read out of the GENERATED assembly
4014               	; 	' -- define_color's `ai r0,>2000` and LDIRVM3's `ai r0,>0800` -- rather
4015               	; 	' than assumed, because a wrong base here would paint over the pattern
4016               	; 	' table and the failure would look like corrupt artwork.
4017               	; 	'
4018               	; 	' Paced: a few hundred VDP writes in one frame are silently dropped.
4019               	; 	' THE SCANNER'S COLOURS ARE THREE BLOCKS REPEATED SIXTEEN TIMES EACH, so
4020               	; 	' the table shipped 384 bytes to say 24 bytes' worth. Same trick as the
4021               	; 	' font: write the colour table directly. >2000 is the colour table's base
4022               	; 	' and >800 the stride between screen thirds -- the same layout DEFINE COLOR
4023               	; 	' walks for us in setup_font, which this cannot use because it is cheaper to
4024               	; 	' expand 24 bytes here than to ship 384 in the bank.
4025               	; 	' NOTHING IS UNDER THE GROUND FLOOR, SO NOTHING SHOULD BE GREEN THERE.
4026               	; 	' A floor bar is five pixels of yellow over three of the green air

4141               	; 	' ======================================================================
4142               	; 	' TITLE
4143               	; 	' ======================================================================
4144               	; 	' DRAWING THE TITLE AND WAITING ON IT ARE TWO ROUTINES, because the boot
4145               	; 	' does something between them: the rest of setup runs while this is on
4146               	; 	' screen. They used to be one, which is why the title could not be shown
4147               	; 	' until everything was ready.
4148               	; 	' THE TITLE IS A DISPLAY LIST IN A ROM BANK, not twelve PRINT ATs.
4149               	; 	'
4150               	; 	' CVBasic embeds a string literal in the FIXED AREA, which is the only
4151               	; 	' budget that cannot be grown -- linkticart writes exactly three loader
4152               	; 	' pages and discards the rest, and they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
4153               	; 	' >A000 rather than cart ROM. 190 characters of title text were sitting
4154               	; 	' in the scarcest place in the program.
4155               	; 	'
4156               	; 	' AND THE REAL POINT IS WHAT IT COSTS NEXT TIME. With the text in a
4157               	; 	' table, changing what the title says or where it sits is an edit to
4158               	; 	' assets/gentitle.py and a rebuild. It costs bank bytes, of which there
4159               	; 	' are thousands, instead of fixed-area bytes, of which there are tens.
4160               	; 	'
4161               	; 	' The table is `row, col, length, bytes...` with 255 to end. ROW AND
4162               	; 	' COLUMN rather than a 16-bit screen offset, because reassembling one
4163               	; 	' from two bytes needs a multiply, and on the TMS9900 MPY clobbers r0 --
4164               	; 	' the next line that reads the product's variable gets the HIGH word
4165               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). Five doublings have no such hazard and are smaller.
4166               	; title_draw:
4167               cvb_TITLE_DRAW
4168               	; 	#if NES
4169               	; 	SCREEN DISABLE
4170               	; 	ASM JSR nes_hats_hide
4171               	; 	' THE TITLE SITS ON DARK BLUE, AND THE BACKDROP IS THE ONLY WAY TO SAY SO.
4172               	; 	'
4173               	; 	' Palette index 0 is the UNIVERSAL backdrop -- every background palette's
4174               	; 	' entry 0 is the same colour, so it cannot be set per region the way the
4175               	; 	' sky and the store are. It was never written at all, which is why every
4176               	; 	' cell that maps to index 0 came out black, the title page included.
4177               	; 	'
4178               	; 	' Writing it here and putting it back in draw_screen costs two statements
4179               	; 	' and no art: the title is almost entirely index 0, so the backdrop IS its
4180               	; 	' background. draw_screen restores grey for buildings, pillars and the
4181               	; 	' scanner margins; black outlines now use palette index 2.
4182               	; 	PALETTE 0,1			' title backdrop
4183               	; 	PALETTE 9,1			' title paper in P2
4184               	; 	WAIT				' hide the clear and restore blue in the same vblank
4185               	; 	' AND EVERY BLOCK ON P2, because the font now has a PAPER.
4186               	; 	'
4187               	; 	' The title's text used to sit on index 0 and index 0 was this backdrop, so
4188               	; 	' it needed no attribute table at all and simply inherited whatever the
4189               	; 	' last game screen left. Now that paper is index 1, "FIRE TO START" would
4190               	; 	' take index 1 of each block it happens to cross -- the store's green under
4191               	; 	' one row, the sunset's orange under another.
4192               	; 	'
4193               	; 	' P2 is the palette that already fits: its index 1 is the same dark blue as
4194               	; 	' the backdrop, so the paper is invisible, and its index 3 is the yellow the
4195               	; 	' logo and the marquee lamps are drawn in. $AA is all four quadrants on P2.
4196               	; 	' draw_screen calls nes_attr and puts the game's own table back.
4197               	; 	#endif

4366               	;
4367               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
4368               	; 	'
4369               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
4370               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
4371               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
4372               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
4373               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
4374               	; 	'
4375               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
4376               	; 	'
4377               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
4378               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,
4379               	; 	'     HardHatMack, Ms. Pac-Man, RallyX, Structris, UFO, Bust-A-Bobble --
4380               	; 	'     and not one has a calibration or has ever shown the fault.
4381               	; 	'   * It never fired on the machine this is developed on: the notice it
4382               	; 	'     prints when it detects a stuck axis has never appeared.
4383               	; 	'   * The original evidence was that the game "came up and would not
4384               	; 	'     start" -- and the first version BLOCKED until the axis cleared. That
4385               	; 	'     symptom is indistinguishable from the several input bugs since found
4386               	; 	'     and fixed for real: keys arriving at a screen that was not listening
4387               	; 	'     yet. The diagnosis was probably one of those.
4388               	; 	'
4389               	; 	' It also cost two bugs of its own: forty frames of a drawn but deaf title
4390               	; 	' screen, which swallowed the first digit of 8-3-8, and a wrong theory

4445               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
4446               	; 	'
4447               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
4448               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
4449               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
4450               	; 	' picture.
4451               	; 	'
4452               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
4453               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
4454               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
4455               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
4456               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
4457               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
4458               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
4459               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
4460               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
4461               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
4462               	; 	' same picture.
4463               	; 	'
4464               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
4465               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
4466               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
4467               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
4468               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.
4469               	; 	bfr = bfr - 1

4487               	; 		' QUEUED, NOT BLANKED -- AND THIS IS WHAT MADE THE TITLE FLASH.
4488               	; 		'
4489               	; 		' nes_def turns rendering OFF and waits for a vblank the NMI
4490               	; 		' therefore never services, so the game's own WAIT then waits for
4491               	; 		' the one after: about two frames with the picture switched off.
4492               	; 		' Twice a marquee step, for ever, on the one screen the player
4493               	; 		' looks at longest. It reads as the whole title flashing, not as
4494               	; 		' the bulbs animating.
4495               	; 		'

4534               	; 		' A SECOND STAGING AREA, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE MARQUEE BUG.
4535               	; 		'
4536               	; 		' nes_escd does NOT copy anything. It builds the tile into the RAM
4537               	; 		' buffer `#nesb` and hands the NMI a five-byte descriptor holding a
4538               	; 		' POINTER to it; the copy happens at the next vblank. Both marquee
4539               	; 		' writes happen in the same pass, so with one buffer the darken call
4540               	; 		' overwrote the staged LIT bytes before the NMI had read either --
4541               	; 		' and then BOTH descriptors copied bulb_off.

4544               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
4545               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
4546               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.
4547               	; 		'
4548               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
4549               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
4550               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
4551               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
4552               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.

4747               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
4748               	; 	'
4749               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
4750               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
4751               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
4752               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
4753               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
4754               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
4755               	; 	'
4756               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
4757               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
4758               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
4759               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
4760               	; 	'
4761               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
4762               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.

5253               	;
5254               	; 	' ======================================================================
5255               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5256               	; 	' ======================================================================
5257               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5258               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5259               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5260               	; 	' of running.
5261               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5262               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5263               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5264               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5265               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5266               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5267               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5268               	; 	'
5269               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5270               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5271               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5272               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5273               	; 	'
5274               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5275               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5276               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5277               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5278               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5279               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5280               	; 	'
5281               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5282               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5283               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5284               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5285               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5286               	; 	'
5287               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5288               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5289               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5290               	; draw_screen:
5291               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN
