5437               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5438               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5439               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5440               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5441               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5442               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5443               	; 	'
5444               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5445               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5446               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5447               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5448               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5449               	; 	'
5450               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5451               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5452               	; 	' above it at all.
5453               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5454               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5455               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5456               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops

6103               	; 			' THEY COME FROM THE FAR SIDE. Kelly walked into this screen

6247               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6248               	; 			'
6249               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6250               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6251               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6252               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6253               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6254               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6255               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6256               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6257               	; 			'
6258               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6259               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6260               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6261               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6262               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6263               	; 			'
6264               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6265               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6266               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6267               	; 			'
6268               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6269               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6270               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6271               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6272               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6273               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.
6274               	; 			' obp is a BALL-only field: upd_obst reads it under an
6275               	; 			' IF uk = OB_BALL and nothing else touches it, and every
6276               	; 			' ball has it computed below. It was seeded here from a
6277               	; 			' table byte that no longer exists, and for anything but
6278               	; 			' a ball that seed was never read.

8701               	;
8702               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8703               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8704               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8705               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8706               	; 	'
8707               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8708               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8709               	; 	'
8710               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8711               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8712               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8713               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8714               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8715               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8716               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8717               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8718               	; 	' merged object.
8719               	; 	'
8720               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8721               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8722               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8723               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8724               	; 	'
8725               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8726               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8727               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8728               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8729               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8730               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8731               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8732               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8733               	; 	'
8734               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8735               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8736               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8737               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8738               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8739               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8740               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8741               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8742               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8743               	; 	'
8744               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8745               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8746               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8747               	; 	#if NES
8748               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8749               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8750               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8751               	; 	'
8752               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8753               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8754               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8755               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8756               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8757               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8758               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
8759               	; 	'
8760               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
8761               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
8762               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
8763               	; 	'
8764               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
8765               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
8766               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
8767               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
8768               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
8769               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
8770               	; 	'                   the whole time.
8771               	; 	'
8772               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
8773               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
8774               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
8775               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
8776               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
8777               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
8778               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
8779               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
8780               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
8781               	; 	'
8782               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
8783               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
8784               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
8785               	; 	' they only need setting once.
8786               	; 	'
8787               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
8788               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
8789               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
8790               	; 	' as him changing pose.
8791               	; nes_swp16:
8792               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
8793               	; 	'
8794               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
8795               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
8796               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
8797               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
8798               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
8799               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
8800               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
8801               	; 	'
8802               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
8803               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
8804               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
8805               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
8806               	; 	'
8807               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
8808               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
8809               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
8810               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
8811               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
8812               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
8813               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
8814               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
8815               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
8816               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2

8843               	;
8844               	; nes_def:
8845               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
8846               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
8847               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
8848               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
8849               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
8850               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
8851               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
8852               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
8853               	; 	RETURN
8854               	;
8855               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
8856               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
8857               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
8858               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
8859               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
8860               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
8861               	; 	'
8862               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
8863               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
8864               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
8865               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
8866               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
8867               	; 	' flashing title screen.
8868               	; 	'
8869               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
8870               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
8871               	; nes_escd:
8872               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrq
8873               	; 	RETURN
8874               	;
8875               	; nes_tpl:
8876               	; 	nti = lv8(nbl)
8877               	; 	nti = nti + klsc
8878               	; 	#ntb = #stix + nti
8879               	; 	ntd = PEEK(#ntb)
8880               	; 	#ntc = #tsrc(ntd)
8881               	; 	#ntc = #ntc + #nta
8882               	; 	#ntc = #ntc + #sttp

8884               	; 	RETURN

9631               	; 	' ======================================================================
9632               	; 	' OBSTACLES
9633               	; 	' ======================================================================
9634               	; upd_obst:
9635               cvb_UPD_OBST
9636               	; 	' ONE ACCUMULATOR PER KIND, NOT PER SLOT. Every hazard of a kind moves at
9637               	; 	' that kind's speed, so three calls a pass serve all eight slots.
9638               	; 	'
9639               	; 	' Per-slot would have meant up to eight calls of O(fdv) work every pass --
9640               	; 	' the positive feedback loop CLAUDE.md 3A warns about, where a slow pass is
9641               	; 	' made slower by the very code meant to take the loop rate out of the
9642               	; 	' game's behaviour. It also saves the eight bytes an obacc() would cost,
9643               	; 	' and ColecoVision RAM is the tighter budget.

9958               	; 	'
9959               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
9960               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
9961               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
9962               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
9963               	; 	'
9964               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
9965               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
9966               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
9967               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
9968               	; 	'
9969               	; 	' Three drains support up to 192/64 units per frame. The remainder
9970               	; 	' is below 64, so the byte addition cannot exceed 255. Planes use
9971               	; 	' two-pixel units and double the result outside this shared routine.
9972               	; 	' Other actors retain pixel units and their existing movement rates.
9973               	; 	'
9974               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
9975               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
9976               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
9977               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
9978               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
9979               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10485               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10486               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10487               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10488               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10489               	; 	' runs every pass.
10490               	; 	'
10491               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10492               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10493               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10494               	; 	'
10495               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10496               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10497               	; 	'
10498               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10499               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10500               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10501               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10502               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10503               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10504               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short

10616               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10617               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10618               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10619               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10620               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10621               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10622               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10623               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10624               	; 	'
10625               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10626               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10627               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10628               	; 	'
10629               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10630               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10631               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10632               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10633               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10634               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10635               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10636               	; 	'
10637               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10638               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10639               	; 	'
10640               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10641               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10642               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10643               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10644               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10645               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10646               	; 	'

10648               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen

10650               	; 	' before any of this.

10653               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10654               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the

11120 D834 0450  20 	b *r0
11121               	;
11122               	; 	' ======================================================================
11123               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11124               	; 	' ======================================================================
11125               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11126               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11127               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11128               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11129               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11130               	; 	'
11131               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11132               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11133               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11134               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11135               	; 	' broken.
11136               	; 	'
11137               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11138               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11139               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11140               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11141               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11142               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11143               	; 	'
11144               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11145               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11146               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11147               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11148               	; coll_obst:
11149               cvb_COLL_OBST

11623               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11624               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11625               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11626               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11627               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11628               	; 	' away from.
11629               	; 	'
11630               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
11631               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
11632               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
11633               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
11634               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --
11635               	; 	' and it left the one hazard that cannot leave on its own as the only one
11636               	; 	' the mercy did not cover. haz_off now takes the characters with it.
11637               	; 	'
11638               	; 	' NOTHING RESTORES IT HERE. load_band repopulates the band from the
11639               	; 	' template, and it runs only on a seam crossing or a round start, so
11640               	; 	' "until the screen is re-entered" costs no state and no timer: leave and
11641               	; 	' come back and the hazards are simply placed again.
11642               	; 	'
11643               	; 	' THE CALL ITSELF IS IN THE MAIN LOOP, at the end of the freeze -- see

11812               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11813               	; 	'
11814               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11815               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11816               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11817               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11818               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11819               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11820               	; 	'
11821               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11822               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11823               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11824               	; 	'
11825               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
11826               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
11827               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
11828               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11829               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11830               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
11831               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.

12517               	; 	' HE IS STRIPED FROM CAP TO HEM. Both stripe colours run the whole upper
12518               	; 	' half, so both boxes span rows 0-15 and neither can be tucked away --
12519               	; 	' affordable only because Kelly's hat moved into a box of its own. His
12520               	; 	' FACE is pushed DOWN instead (hy+3, box 3..18) so it clears the cap
12521               	; 	' rows, where his two stripe boxes plus Kelly's hat and face already
12522               	; 	' make four. Worst line of a meeting: exactly four, nothing dropped.
12523               	; 	' HE RISES A PIXEL ON THE RECOVERY BEATS. A runner is highest at mid-flight
12524               	; 	' and lowest at contact; with the body pinned at a constant y, alternating
12525               	; 	' legs under a motionless torso reads as a dance rather than as travel.
12526               	; 	'
12527               	; 	' One pixel is enough at this size, and it lifts the BODY ONLY -- the legs
12528               	; 	' keep their y, so the planted foot stays on the floor and the figure
12529               	; 	' stretches at the waist instead of hopping. Lifting the legs too would be
12530               	; 	' a jump.
12531               	; 	'
12532               	; 	' Beats 2 and 4 are the recoveries, which is exactly `hanim AND 8` -- the
12533               	; 	' cycle's LOW beat bit. IT MUST MOVE WITH THE BEAT BITS ABOVE IT: on the
12534               	; 	' wrong bit he rises and falls twice per stride, a second clock inside one
12535               	; 	' figure, which is the flapping of DESIGN.md 0j2 in the vertical.
12536               	; 	'
12537               	; 	' Safe because HARRY'S COLLISION HAS NO VERTICAL COMPONENT: he is caught on
12538               	; 	' `same level AND |dx| < CATCHR`. Doing this to Kelly would desynchronise
12539               	; 	' his sprite from the ball and biplane windows in DESIGN.md 5a, which is
12540               	; 	' why it is not done to him.
12541               	; 	' THE WHOLE FIGURE RISES, legs included, rather than the body stretching
12542               	; 	' away from the feet. Two reasons, and the second was not the first plan:
12543               	; 	'
12544               	; 	'   * It is what a run does. Mid-flight BOTH feet are off the ground, so

13011               	; 	' ======================================================================
13012               	; 	' THE SCANNER
13013               	; 	' ======================================================================
13014               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13015               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
13016               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
13017               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13018               	; 	'
13019               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
13020               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13021               	; 	'
13022               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13023               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13024               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13025               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13026               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13027               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13028               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13029               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13030               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13031               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13032               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.
13033               	; esc_tick:
13034               cvb_ESC_TICK

13036               	; 	' entirely -- which is what makes rewriting the cells every frame

13038               	; 	' miscompiles a compare-AND-compare (CLAUDE.md 3A).

13058               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13059               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13060               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13061               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13062               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13063               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13064               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13065               	; 	'
13066               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13067               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13068               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13069               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13070               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13071               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13072               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

13086               	; 	#if NES
13087               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13088               	; 	'
13089               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13090               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13091               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13092               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13093               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13094               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13095               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13096               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13097               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13098               	; 	'
13099               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13100               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13101               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13102               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13103               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13104               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13105               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13106               	; 	'
13107               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13108               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13109               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13110               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13111               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13112               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13113               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13114               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13115               	; 	' with room to spare.
13116               	; 	'
13117               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13118               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13119               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13120               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13121               	; 	WAIT
13122               	; 	#endif
13123               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13124               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13125               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13126               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13127               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13128               	; 	'
13129               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13130               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13131               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13132               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13133               	; 	'
13134               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13135               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13136               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13137               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13138               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13139               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13140               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13141               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13142               	; 	'
13143               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never
13144               	; 	' move at all.
13145               	; 	IF klsc = 0 THEN

13472               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
13473               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is

13477               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
13478               	; 	'
13479               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level

13482               	; 	'

13484               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
13485               	; 	'   +2  GREY

13489               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all

13944               	;
13945               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13946               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
13947               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13948               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13949               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13950               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13951               	; scan_wipe:
13952               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
13953               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13954               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13955               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13956               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13957               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13958               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13959               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13960               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13961               	; 	'
13962               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13963               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13964               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13965               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13966               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13967               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13968               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
13969               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
13970               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13971               	; 	'
13972               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13973               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
13974               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
13975               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
13976               	; 	'
13977               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
13978               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.
13979               	; 	#swa = 5760			' 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8, the canvas patterns

     E8E0 1680

     E8E4 20E8

14072               	;
14073               	; 	' THE TWO ACTORS ARE SPRITES; EVERYTHING ELSE IS CHARACTERS.
14074               	; 	'
14075               	; 	' That split is what makes the instrument simple. The floor lines, the
14076               	; 	' flights and the lift car do not move relative to the canvas, so they
14077               	; 	' are pixels in the scanner's own characters and cost nothing to keep.
14078               	; 	' The Kop and the crook DO move, and as sprites they need no colour
14079               	; 	' table, no erase and no priority arithmetic -- they draw over the
14080               	; 	' furniture because sprites always do, and nothing shifts to make room.
14081               	; 	'
14082               	; 	' IT ALSO REMOVED THE BLINK. Kelly flashed because a pixel row of this
14083               	; 	' canvas can only carry one colour, so at close range the two markers
14084               	; 	' merged and the blink was the only thing left to tell them apart. Two
14085               	; 	' sprites are two colours wherever they stand.
14086               	; 	'
14087               	; 	' The furniture is drawn ONCE, by scan_furn. It used to be redrawn every
14088               	; 	' tick because erasing a character-based marker ANDed bits out of
14089               	; 	' whatever it was standing on; there is nothing left to rub it away. The
14090               	; 	' car still redraws itself, because the car actually moves.
14091               	; 	' -- the lift car. IT WAS FLICKERING, and the cause was not the drawing
14092               	; 	' but the ERASING: scan_elev cleared its three cells and put them back
14093               	; 	' every tick, whether or not the car had moved, so several times a second
14094               	; 	' there was a window with the pixels off. A sprite has no erase at all --
14095               	; 	' it is placed, and the VDP does the rest -- and slot 26 sits BELOW the
14096               	; 	' two markers, so the Kop and the crook pass over it without either of
14097               	; 	' them having to know the car exists.

15155               	;
15156               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15157               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15158               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15159               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15160               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15161               	; 	'
15162               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15163               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15164               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15165               	; 	'
15166               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15167               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15168               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15169               	; 	'
15170               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15171               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15172               	; 	'
15173               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15174               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15175               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15176               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15177               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15178               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15179               	; 	'
15180               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15181               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15182               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15183               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15184               	; 	'
15185               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15186               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15187               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15188               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
15189               	; bonus_count:

15332               	;
15333               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15334               	; 	'
15335               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15336               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15337               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15338               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15339               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15340               	; 	'
15341               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15342               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15343               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15344               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15345               	; 	' counting stops.
15346               	;
15347               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15348               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15349               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15350               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15351               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15352               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15353               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15354               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15355               	; 	'
15356               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15357               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15358               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).

15407               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout

15417               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
15418               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store

15707               	;
15708               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15709               	; 	'
15710               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15711               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15712               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15713               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15714               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15715               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15716               	; 	'
15717               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15718               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15719               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15720               	; 	'
15721               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15722               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15723               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15724               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15725               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15726               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15727               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15728               	; 	'
15729               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15730               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15731               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15732               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15733               	; 	'
15734               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15735               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15736               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15737               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15738               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15739               	; 	'
15740               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15741               	; 	' did not finish.
15742               	; pause_beat:
15743               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT

15745 F1C0 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F1C2 A980

15750               	; 	' call sites would have cost code to say the same thing worse.
15751               	; 	'
15752               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNT AND NOT THE WAITS. sfx_tick runs once per pass, so it
15753               	; 	' would tick half as often per frame if the three WAITs became six -- the

15896               	; 	' A PRIZE IS AN ARPEGGIO -- testsounds PICKUP C. C5, E5, G5, then a fade
15897               	; 	' on the top note: it RISES, which is what makes it read as a reward
15898               	; 	' rather than as an event, and it ARRIVES, because a major triad resolves
15899               	; 	' where an arbitrary rise just stops.
15900               	; 	'
15901               	; 	' It was two notes struck together on two channels and held. That needed
15902               	; 	' both channels for one sound, said nothing in particular, and had no
15903               	; 	' shape at all -- a chord is a texture, and this wants to be a phrase.
15904               	; 	'

16174               	;
16175               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16176               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16177               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16178               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16179               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16180               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16181               	;
16182               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16183               	; 	'
16184               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16185               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16186               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16187               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16188               	; 	'
16189               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16190               	; 	'
16191               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16192               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16193               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16194               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16195               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16196               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16197               	; 	'
16198               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16199               	; 	'
16200               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16201               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16202               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16203               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16204               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16205               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16206               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16207               	; 	'
16208               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16209               	; 	'
16210               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16211               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16212               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16213               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16214               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16215               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16216               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16217               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16218               	; 	'
16219               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16220               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16221               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16222               	; 	'
16223               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16224               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16225               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16226               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16227               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16228               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16229               	; 	'
16230               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16231               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16232               	; 	'
16233               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16234               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16235               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16236               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16237               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16238               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16239               	; 	'
16240               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16241               	; 	'
16242               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16243               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16244               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
16245               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
16246               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
16247               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not

16573               	;
16574               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16575               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16576               	; 	'
16577               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16578               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16579               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16580               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16581               	; 	'
16582               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16583               	; 	'
16584               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16585               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16586               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16587               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16588               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16589               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16590               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16591               	; 	'
16592               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16593               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16594               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16595               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16596               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16597               	; 	'
16598               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16599               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16600               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16601               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16602               	; 	#if TI994A
16603               	; 	BANK 2
16604      0958     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$

17692               	;
17693               	; 	' THE COLOUR TABLE, 472 bytes of the same value ($B4 = light yellow ink on dark blue).
17694               	; 	'
17695               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col, which is ONE synchronous call that
17696               	; 	' writes all three screen thirds (define_color always does the LDIRVM3 triple
17697               	; 	' copy). It replaced a VPOKE loop that wrote this one value 1,416 times paced by
17698               	; 	' 24 WAITs -- the largest scripted delay in the boot, and the reason the title
17699               	; 	' screen used to fill in visibly rather than appearing at once.
17700               	; 	'
17701               	; 	' EIGHT BYTES PER CHARACTER, not one. Supply fewer and DEFINE COLOR reads
17702               	; 	' whatever follows in ROM as colour data, with no error at build or run time.
17703               	;
17704               	; #if NES
17705               	; 	' NES uses nes_fcol; omit this identical 472-byte TMS colour table.
17706               	; #else
17707               	; font_col:
17708               cvb_FONT_COL

18155               	; 	' Generated by assets/gentitle.py -- do not edit here.

18440               	; 	INCLUDE "art.bas"
18441               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
18442               	; 	'
18443               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
18444               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
18445               	; 	' being small sprites.
18446               	; 	'
18447               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
18448               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
18449               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
18450               	; 	'
18451               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
18452               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
18453               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
18454               	;
18455               	; spr_kelly:	' Kelly: RIGHT hat/face/two merged run bodies/two FREE slots/duck hat/face/body, then the same LEFT (+36). The run bodies carry tunic AND legs, so a frame is one sprite, and standing is run frame 1. Patterns 0..68
18456               cvb_SPR_KELLY

19687               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
19688               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
19689               	; 	'
19690               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
19691               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
19692               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
19693               	; 	'
19694               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
19695               	; 	' blit is
19696               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
19697               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
19698               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
19699               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
19700               	; 	'
19701               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
19702               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
19703               	; 	'
19704               	; 	' template ids:
19705               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
19706               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
19707               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
19708               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
19709               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
19710               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
19711               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
19712               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2
19713               	; 	'   8 T_ROOF3
19714               	; 	'   9 T_ROOF4
19715               	; 	'   10 T_ROOF5
19716               	; 	'   11 T_ROOF6
19717               	; 	'   12 T_ROOF7
19718               	; 	'   13 T_END_W
19719               	; 	'   14 T_END_E
19720               	;
19721               	; stor_tpl:	' 15 templates x 160 bytes
19722               cvb_STOR_TPL

20337               	;
20338               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
20339               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
20340               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
20341               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
20342               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
20343               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
20344               	; #if NES
20345               	; nes_sky2c:
20346               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
20347               	; nes_bldlc:
20348               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
20349               	; #endif
20350               	;
20351               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
20352               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
20353               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
20354               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
20355               	; 	'
20356               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
20357               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
20358               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
20359               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).
